bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay

If you earn an hourly wage or have a salary offer, the first step is to calculate your annual gross pay. The standard formula is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

For a full-time employee, we assume 38 hours per week, as set by the Fair Work Ombudsman. So if your hourly rate is $30.00, your annual pay would be:

$30.00 × 38 × 52 = $59,280

This calculation gives you a baseline figure. It assumes you work the same hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. If you are a casual employee, remember that your hourly rate often includes a 25% casual loading. On [the timesheet](/), you can enter your base hourly rate and then check a box to add the loading on top – never type a rate that already includes casual loading.

Knowing your annual figure helps you compare job offers, plan your budget, and understand your fortnightly pay. A fortnight is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two. For the example above, weekly pay is $1,140, so fortnightly pay is $2,280 before tax and super.

## National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage (NMW) is the legal minimum for employees not covered by an award or agreement. From 1 July 2026, the NMW is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Casual employees get $33.05 per hour including the 25% loading.

However, most Australian workers are covered by a modern award or enterprise agreement, which often sets higher minimum rates. For example, a retail employee under the General Retail Industry Award may earn more than the NMW. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) for each award, listing the specific rates for different classifications. These award rates are not job medians – they are minimum standards. If you are looking for typical earnings in your occupation, the Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes average weekly earnings. For May 2026, full-time adult ordinary time earnings averaged $2,083.70 per week, while all employees (including part-time) averaged $1,579.20 per week. These are averages, not medians for a specific job.

When comparing a salary offer to your current hourly rate, always check whether the offer is above the relevant award rate. If you are a casual, your hourly rate should include the 25% loading on top of the base award rate. You can use [reference tables](/data) to see common award classifications.

## Understanding Tax and Superannuation

Once you have your annual gross pay, you need to estimate tax and super. The Australian Taxation Office sets the resident tax rates for 2026–27 as follows:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

In addition, most residents pay a 2% Medicare levy. The Medicare levy reduction thresholds used here are from 2025–26, as the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of this guide. Other deductions like HELP loans, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not included in this estimate.

Superannuation is paid on top of your salary. The super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to a maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For example, if your annual gross pay is $60,000, your employer must contribute an extra $7,200 into your super fund. This super is not part of your take-home pay – it is an additional benefit. You can see your estimated take-home pay after tax and Medicare on our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page.

## How Much to Salary Sacrifice into Super

Salary sacrifice is a way to boost your super by directing some of your pre-tax salary into your super fund. This reduces your taxable income, so you pay less income tax now. The contributions are taxed at 15% within super (up to the concessional cap), which is often lower than your marginal tax rate.

So, how much to salary sacrifice into super? It depends on your income, your tax bracket, and your retirement goals. For example, if you earn $80,000 per year and salary sacrifice $5,000, your taxable income drops to $75,000. You save tax at your marginal rate of 30% (plus 2% Medicare) on that $5,000, meaning you keep more of your money in super rather than paying it to the ATO. However, you must stay within the annual concessional contributions cap (including your employer’s contributions) to avoid extra tax.

To decide how much to salary sacrifice, first calculate your annual pay using the formula above. Then consider your tax bracket and how much you can afford to put away. The Australian Taxation Office provides guidance on caps and rules. You can also discuss with your employer or a financial adviser. Remember, salary sacrifice is voluntary and not included in the standard pay estimate on this site.

## Putting It All Together

Converting your hourly rate to annual pay is straightforward: multiply by hours per week and 52. For a full-time 38-hour week, that gives you a gross figure. Then subtract estimated tax and Medicare to get take-home pay, and add 12% super on top. If you are a casual, remember the 25% loading is already part of your hourly rate – do not double-count it.

Whether you are comparing a salary offer or checking your current wage, always refer to the relevant award or the National Minimum Wage. The Fair Work Ombudsman’s [pay guides](/blog) are the best source for award rates. For average earnings, see the [average pay](/topics/average-pay) page. And if you are considering salary sacrifice, think about how much to salary sacrifice into super based on your personal circumstances.

This guide provides an estimate only. Your actual pay may vary due to overtime, allowances, or other factors. Always consult a qualified professional for personal financial advice.
